blocks.text: When you first build an agent, it is tempting to put everything inside one big loop, think, call a tool, look at the result, think again, repeat. That works for small demos but it quickly becomes unpredictable once the task has several distinct stages.

A workflow gives an agent task an explicit shape, a sequence of named steps, with clear points where the agent branches on a condition or loops until something is true. MCP tool calls slot neatly into each step, and because each step is named, you get real visibility into what the agent is doing right now.

This lesson walks through the common workflow shapes, shows where MCP tool calls fit inside each step, and builds a small workflow engine you can actually run, including simple observability so you always know which step is active.
1. Why Structure Beats One Giant Loop

blocks.alt: A structured workflow is compared against one giant loop

blocks.text: A single unstructured loop asks the model to decide everything on every turn, what to do next, whether it is done, whether something went wrong. That puts a lot of weight on one prompt.

An explicit workflow moves some of that decision making out of the prompt and into code you control. The model still reasons inside each step, but the shape of the task, what comes after what, lives outside the model.

blocks.title: A workflow is just a state machine
blocks.content: Underneath the agent language, a workflow is a small state machine, a current step, a set of allowed transitions, and a place to store results so later steps can use them.

blocks.text: This separation matters most when a task grows past two or three tool calls. At that point, unstructured loops tend to repeat work, skip steps, or get stuck without anyone noticing.
Structure also makes a task easier to hand off. A teammate reading a workflow definition can see the shape of the task in seconds, without reading every prompt the agent might send.
2. Sequential Steps, the Simplest Shape

blocks.alt: Step one leads to step two which leads to step three

blocks.text: The most basic workflow shape is a straight line, step one finishes, its output feeds step two, step two finishes, its output feeds step three.
Each step has one job. A step that both searches for data and writes the final answer is really two steps pretending to be one, and it is harder to observe or retry.

items: Step: gather requirements from the user request
Step: call an MCP tool to fetch the data needed
Step: transform or summarize the fetched data
Step: produce the final response

blocks.text: Sequential steps are easy to test in isolation too, since each one takes a known input and produces a known output, independent of the steps around it.
Because sequential steps have no branching, they are also the easiest shape to log. A developer can simply print the step name as it starts and confirm it finished before moving on.
3. Branching on a Condition

blocks.alt: A condition branches the workflow down one of two paths

blocks.text: Sometimes the next step depends on what an earlier step found. A branch checks a condition and sends the workflow down one of two or more paths.
Good branch conditions are simple and checkable in code, not another open ended model call. For example, checking whether a tool result list is empty is a plain condition, no reasoning required.
Keep the number of branches small. A workflow with ten possible branches is usually a sign the task should be broken into smaller workflows instead.
A branch step should never call an MCP tool on its own. It only reads results that an earlier step already fetched and decides where to go next.
4. Loops That Repeat Until a Criteria Is Met

blocks.alt: A loop repeats a step until a criteria is finally met

blocks.text: A loop step repeats the same step, or a small group of steps, until some criteria is satisfied, then hands control to the next step in the workflow.
The criteria must be checkable without asking the model again, otherwise the loop can spin forever if the model keeps giving an ambiguous answer.

blocks.title: Always cap loop iterations
blocks.content: Every loop needs a hard maximum iteration count, even when the exit criteria looks reliable. A capped loop fails loudly and safely, an uncapped loop can run forever and burn tool calls.

items: Loop until a search returns at least one usable result
Loop until a generated draft passes a validation check
Loop until a paginated MCP resource has no more pages left

blocks.text: Each pass through the loop should also increment a counter that lives outside the model entirely, so the cap is enforced no matter what the model says about being done.
5. Where MCP Tool Calls Fit Inside a Step

blocks.alt: An MCP tool call sits inside one workflow step

blocks.text: An MCP tool call almost always lives inside the body of a single step, never spread across several steps. The step calls the tool, waits for the result, and stores it for whatever comes next.
Thinking of it this way keeps the workflow easy to read, a step named fetch_ticket_details clearly means one MCP tool call happens right there.
A step does not have to call a tool at all. Plan and summarize steps usually just reason over context already stored from earlier steps, with no MCP call involved.
When a step does call a tool, it should call exactly one, or a small fixed set. A step that dynamically decides which of ten tools to call is really a workflow hiding inside a single step.
6. Designing Clear Step Boundaries
A well designed step has a name, a clear input it reads from context, and a clear output it writes back to context. Nothing else should leak between steps.
If two steps need to share a piece of state that is not obvious from their names, that is usually a sign one of them is doing too much.
7. Building a Small Workflow Engine
Rather than hardcoding the order of steps in one long function, a workflow engine reads a list of step definitions and runs them in order, handling branches and loops as it goes.
Each step definition is small, just a name, a type such as task, branch, or loop, and the function that does the actual work.
Notice retry_fetch reuses the same function as fetch_data. Steps are just named entries pointing at reusable functions, they do not need unique logic every time.
8. Running the Engine With Observability Hooks
The engine keeps a pointer to the current step name and calls an onStepChange hook every time it moves, which is exactly the hook a developer uses to see progress live.
The loopCount guard is the hard cap discussed earlier, applied at the engine level so no single branch definition can forget it.
9. Wiring MCP Tool Calls Into the Engine
A task step that needs an MCP tool simply calls the shared MCP client inside its run function, then returns whatever the next step will need.
The branch function above never calls a tool itself, it only reads a result that a previous step already stored. Keeping branches free of tool calls makes them fast and easy to test.
10. Observability Into a Running Workflow
At minimum, a developer watching a running workflow needs three things, which step is active right now, how long each step took, and whether a step succeeded or failed.

items: Current step name and status, running, done, or failed
Timestamp when each step started and finished
Which tool, if any, the step called and what it returned
How many times a loop step has repeated so far

blocks.text: None of this requires a heavy monitoring stack. A simple structured log line per step, written wherever your other logs go, is usually enough to answer where is my agent stuck.
11. Storing State So You Can Inspect It Later

blocks.alt: Workflow state is stored so it can be inspected later

blocks.text: A running workflow should keep its current step name and full context somewhere a developer can query, not only in memory that disappears when the process exits.
For a long running agent, that usually means writing the context object to a database row after every step, keyed by a workflow run id.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["run_id","Unique id for this workflow execution"],["current_step","Name of the step currently running or last completed"],["status","running, done, or failed"],["context","Full stored results from every completed step"]]}

blocks.text: With this stored, a developer, or a status page, can answer which step is my agent on right now with a single lookup instead of tailing logs.
12. Combining Branches and Loops in One Workflow
Real workflows rarely use just one shape. A typical support agent workflow fetches data, loops until enough results come back, then branches on whether a human handoff is needed.

items: plan, a single task step
fetch_data, looped up to a small maximum
check_results, a branch deciding retry versus continue
needs_human, a branch deciding escalate versus summarize
summarize or escalate, the two possible final task steps

blocks.text: Even with five steps and two branches, the workflow stays readable because every step still has exactly one job.
13. Handling Errors Inside a Step

blocks.alt: An error inside one step is caught before it breaks the whole workflow

blocks.text: An MCP tool call inside a step can fail, a timeout, a bad argument, a server error. The step should catch that failure and turn it into a normal outcome the engine understands.
A following branch step can then check outcome.error and route to a retry step or a graceful failure message, instead of letting the whole workflow crash.
14. Worked Example, a Support Ticket Workflow
Picture an agent that answers a question about a support ticket. The workflow plans the query, fetches the ticket over MCP, loops if nothing comes back yet, then summarizes.
Running this with the loop cap in place means a missing ticket eventually fails cleanly after ten attempts, rather than hanging the agent forever.
15. Common Mistakes
A few mistakes show up again and again when developers first move from a single loop to an explicit workflow.

items: Putting an MCP tool call inside a branch function, mixing decision logic with side effects
Forgetting a maximum iteration count on a loop, letting a bad condition spin forever
Letting two steps silently share hidden state instead of passing it through context
Logging only errors and not the step transitions, so a stuck workflow looks identical to a working one
Building one giant step that both calls a tool and decides the next branch, losing the benefit of clear boundaries

blocks.text: 16. Practice
Take the support ticket workflow above and add a new branch after summarize, one that checks whether the ticket status is closed and, if not, adds an escalate step.

items: Add an escalate_step function that logs a message and returns a final result
Wire it in as a new branch target from checkTicketBranch
Add an onStepChange hook that prints the step name and status to the console
Run the workflow with a ticket that is never found and confirm the loop cap stops it after ten tries

blocks.text: 17. Key Takeaway

An explicit workflow turns a fuzzy multi step agent task into a small set of named steps with clear inputs, outputs, and transitions. MCP tool calls live inside individual steps, branches decide what comes next using plain checkable conditions, and loops repeat with a hard cap until real criteria are met.

The small payoff for this structure is observability. Because every step has a name and reports its own status, a developer can always answer which step is my agent on right now, instead of guessing from a wall of unstructured log lines.
